This vignette shows how to display cortical geometry, curvature, and vertex
values with RGL. It uses the small `std.8` surfaces bundled with neurosurf,
so no downloads are needed. Every RGL scene below is an interactive WebGL
widget: drag to rotate, scroll to zoom. Static figures use neurosurf's CPU
renderer, which needs no OpenGL.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.4, out.width = "100%")
```

The `std.8` template has 642 vertices per hemisphere, about 10 mm apart. RGL
colours each vertex and blends across triangles, so on a mesh this coarse a
thresholded map gets jagged edges. One round of Loop subdivision
(2,562 vertices) is enough for display:

```{r load}
library(neurosurf)

refine <- function(geometry) {
  mesh <- Rvcg::vcgSubdivide(geometry@mesh, threshold = 0,
                             type = "Loop", iterations = 1,
                             silent = TRUE)
  SurfaceGeometry(t(mesh$vb[1:3, ]), t(mesh$it) - 1L, geometry@hemi)
}
std8 <- load_fsaverage_std8("smoothwm")
left <- refine(smooth(std8$lh, type = "HCLaplace", delta = 0.2,
                      iteration = 5))
right <- refine(smooth(std8$rh, type = "HCLaplace", delta = 0.2,
                       iteration = 5))
inflated_lh <- refine(load_fsaverage_std8("inflated")$lh)
```

For values, two smooth clusters of opposite sign stand in for a statistic
map. Each is placed at a surface coordinate and falls off with distance over
the inflated surface, which follows the cortical sheet:

```{r values}
blob <- function(centre, peak, width = 15) {
  seed <- which.min(colSums((t(coords(left)) - centre)^2))
  xyz <- coords(inflated_lh)
  peak * exp(-colSums((t(xyz) - xyz[seed, ])^2) / (2 * width^2))
}
vertex_values <- blob(c(-45, -60, 20), 3) +  # parietal, positive
  blob(c(-55, -20, 0), -2.5)                 # temporal, negative
```

## Open a scene and show it

`view_surface()` draws into the current RGL device when `new_window = FALSE`.
This helper gives each example a private NULL device, returns the scene as a
WebGL widget, and closes the device even if the plotting call fails. In an
interactive session, use `rgl::open3d()` to get a desktop window instead.

```{r scene-helper}
with_rgl_scene <- function(code) {
  device <- rgl::open3d(useNULL = TRUE)
  on.exit(rgl::close3d(device), add = TRUE)
  force(code)
  rgl::rglwidget()
}
```

A `SurfaceGeometry` records its hemisphere, so `viewpoint = "lateral"`
selects the appropriate left or right view. By default the surface is shaded
by its curvature, sulci dark and gyri light; `bgcol` replaces that base
colour.

```{r basic-plot}
with_rgl_scene(
  view_surface(left, viewpoint = "lateral", zoom = 0.8,
               new_window = FALSE)
)
```

## Overlay values

Pass vertex values in `vals`. `irange` sets the colour limits and
`thresh = c(-1, 1)` leaves values inside that band uncoloured, so the
curvature shows through. Signed values get neurosurf's diverging palette,
`surface_palette("two_sided")`: blue below zero, red above, with no white
centre to fade into the grey anatomy. Pass `cmap` to choose another.

```{r data-overlay}
with_rgl_scene(
  view_surface(left, vals = vertex_values, irange = c(-3, 3),
               thresh = c(-1, 1), viewpoint = "lateral", zoom = 0.8,
               new_window = FALSE)
)
```

For a static figure with a colour key, use `surface_figure()`. It renders
the same values with the CPU renderer, which interpolates within each
triangle, so its lighting and colour mapping do not depend on RGL.

```{r static-overlay}
figure <- surface_figure(
  lh = left, values = vertex_values, anatomy = curvature(left),
  views = "lateral", threshold = 1, limits = c(-3, 3),
  legend_title = "value", panel_width = 640, panel_height = 380,
  antialias = 2
)
```

```{r overlay-image, echo=FALSE, out.width="80%", fig.align="center"}
file <- knitr::fig_path("overlay.png")
dir.create(dirname(file), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
write_surface_figure(figure, file)
knitr::include_graphics(file)
```

## Vertex colours

`vert_clrs` supplies one explicit colour per vertex and overrides scalar
colour mapping, for example to show a parcellation. Here the anterior half of
the hemisphere (positive y) is green and the posterior half purple. `alpha`
blends these colours with the curvature shading beneath, so the folds stay
visible.

```{r vertex-colors}
y <- coords(left)[, 2]
halves <- ifelse(y > median(y), "#1b7837", "#762a83")
with_rgl_scene(
  view_surface(left, vert_clrs = halves, alpha = 0.6,
               viewpoint = "lateral", zoom = 0.8, new_window = FALSE)
)
```

`specular` sets the highlight colour (the default `"black"` gives a matte
surface), and `lit` turns lighting on or off. These change the displayed
scene, not the stored geometry or vertex data.

## Combine hemispheres in one scene

The two lateral surfaces face opposite directions, so show them in separate
panels. A dorsal view sees both hemispheres at once, so they can share one
scene; `offset` separates them along x.

```{r two-hemispheres}
with_rgl_scene({
  view_surface(left, viewpoint = "dorsal", offset = c(-5, 0, 0),
               new_window = FALSE)
  view_surface(right, viewpoint = "dorsal", offset = c(5, 0, 0),
               new_window = FALSE)
})
```

Other views are `"medial"`, `"ventral"`, `"anterior"` and `"posterior"`. For
static multi-view output, `surface_figure()` combines hemispheres and labels
each view; see `vignette("surface-figures")`.

## Mark vertices and plot a surface data object

`NeuroSurface` stores values with the vertex indices they belong to. Here it
holds only the suprathreshold vertices, and its `plot()` method passes them
to `view_surface()`. Markers refer to vertices too: these sit on the peak
vertex of each cluster.

```{r surface-object}
active <- which(abs(vertex_values) > 1)
surface <- NeuroSurface(left, indices = active,
                        data = vertex_values[active])
peaks <- data.frame(
  vertex = c(which.max(vertex_values), which.min(vertex_values)),
  radius = 2.5, color = "#1f2933"
)
with_rgl_scene(
  plot(surface, irange = c(-3, 3), spheres = peaks,
       spheres_as_vertices = TRUE, viewpoint = "lateral", zoom = 0.8,
       new_window = FALSE)
)
```

## Smooth and threshold a noisy map

Smoothing and cluster-size thresholding operate on surface data before
rendering. Here noise is added to the two clusters, averaged over a 10 mm
geodesic radius (`sigma`), and thresholded at |value| > 1, keeping only
connected clusters of at least 20 vertices. Smoothing recovers the two known
clusters and removes the speckle.

```{r activation-map}
set.seed(123)
noise <- rnorm(length(vertex_values))
noisy <- NeuroSurface(left, indices = nodes(left),
                      data = vertex_values + noise)
smoothed <- smooth(noisy, sigma = 10)
clustered <- cluster_threshold(smoothed, size = 20,
                               threshold = c(-1, 1))
```

Shown as small multiples with one colour scale:

```{r activation-panels}
steps <- list(noisy = noisy, smoothed = smoothed,
              clustered = clustered)
panels <- lapply(steps, function(x) {
  render_surface_rgba(left, as.numeric(x@data), camera = "lateral",
                      threshold = 1, limits = c(-3, 3),
                      width = 420, height = 260, antialias = 2)
})
```

```{r activation-image, echo=FALSE, fig.width=7.5, fig.height=1.9, fig.cap="Left lateral view of the same values at each step; |value| &gt; 1 is coloured, limits &plusmn;3, blue negative, red positive."}
grid::grid.newpage()
grid::pushViewport(grid::viewport(layout = grid::grid.layout(
  2, 3, heights = grid::unit(c(1, 1.5), c("null", "lines"))
)))
for (j in seq_along(panels)) {
  rgba <- panels[[j]]$rgba
  grid::grid.raster(array(as.numeric(rgba) / 255, dim = dim(rgba)),
                    vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 1, layout.pos.col = j))
  grid::grid.text(names(panels)[j],
                  gp = grid::gpar(fontsize = 10, col = "#333333"),
                  vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 2, layout.pos.col = j))
}
```

`surface_montage()` lays out RGL snapshots the same way; it needs a
rendering backend, so it is not run here:

```{r montage, eval=FALSE}
surface_montage(list(noisy, smoothed, clustered), irange = c(-3, 3),
                thresh = c(-1, 1), ncol = 3)
```

## Save an RGL snapshot

`snapshot_surface()` saves a PNG through the available RGL rendering backend.
On a NULL device it needs webshot2 and a headless browser, and it returns an
empty path when no snapshot could be made. Building this article does not
launch a browser, so this recipe is not run here:

```{r snapshot, eval=FALSE}
file <- tempfile(fileext = ".png")
path <- snapshot_surface(left, file = file, vals = vertex_values,
                         irange = c(-3, 3), viewpoint = "lateral")
```

For browser-free PNG output, use `surface_figure()` or
`render_surface_rgba()`. For interactive reports with several selectable
maps, see `vignette("interactive-surfaces")`.

The bundled templates retain the FreeSurfer terms in
`system.file("extdata", "LICENSE-FreeSurfer.txt", package = "neurosurf")`.
